Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Authority Presence: Police, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Arjun was 41, a married South Asian graphic designer who had built his life around careful routines, client deadlines, and the quiet order of his apartment in the city. Before the event, he was the kind of person who could spend hours refining a layout, moving a line by a few millimetres until it felt right. That sense of control had changed after a police-related incident that he still struggled to name in full. He could say what happened in outline, but when he tried to tell the story in detail, he lost the thread and found himself stopping mid-sentence, frustrated and embarrassed. Even in therapy, he would start with a clear beginning and then trail off, saying that he knew it happened, knew the sequence in his head, but could not find the words to make it come out properly.

The event itself remained vivid in fragments. Arjun remembered being confronted by police officers, and he remembered the presence of uniformed people as something that instantly narrowed his attention and tightened his body. What had made the memory so difficult for him was not only the authority of the officers, but the sense that someone he had trusted had betrayed him in that setting. He spoke of that betrayal with a flat, wounded certainty: he had expected one thing from a person he trusted, and instead found himself exposed and unsafe. Since then, when he remembers the event, he feels intense guilt. He returns to the same painful thought that he should have seen it coming or handled it differently, even though he can only describe that regret in short pieces before he becomes stuck. The memory is not a neat narrative in his mind; it is a sequence of scenes, sensations, and unfinished sentences that leave him feeling as though he is failing even to explain his own experience.

In the months after, ordinary parts of the day became strangely charged. A burnt smell was one of the most immediate reminders. He noticed it first when food was left too long on the stove in the apartment kitchen, then again outside the building when a neighbour’s cooking drifted through the hallway. The smell would pull him back into the event with little warning, making the present feel suddenly unsafe and contaminated by what had happened before. He became vigilant for dangerous people, scanning faces and posture in a way that felt automatic to him. On his commute and in the lobby of the office building, he watched for anyone in uniform, and a police car parked at the curb could unsettle him enough that he would change his route or linger until it moved on. People in authority, especially anyone in a uniform, now carried that same charge for him. He found himself studying them before they noticed him, already preparing for the worst.

At work, these changes showed up in practical ways. As a graphic designer, Arjun regularly met with clients, printers, and building staff, and before any interaction he began rehearsing conversations in his head. He would draft responses in advance, run through possible questions, and rehearse what he might say if he was challenged or misunderstood. He told himself this was simply being prepared, but it also reflected how difficult it had become for him to trust that an exchange would stay ordinary. If a delivery person wore a uniform or if a client mentioned calling security, he felt his attention sharpen and his body tense. He sat nearer to exits in meetings and checked hallways more often than before, not because he believed danger was certain in every moment, but because he no longer felt comfortable assuming he would recognize it too late.

He also began avoiding any future plans. Where he once discussed travel with his wife or thought ahead to projects months in advance, he now hesitated, reluctant to commit to anything that depended on the world remaining predictable. Planning, for Arjun, had started to feel like inviting disappointment or putting himself in a position where he could be cornered again. This shift affected his marriage in small but noticeable ways. His wife would ask about holidays, family visits, or even weekend arrangements, and he would answer vaguely or change the subject, leaving decisions open longer than before. The uncertainty was easier for him than the feeling of being trapped by a plan he might later regret.

By the time he sought help, Arjun was weary of living in a state of guardedness. He had become increasingly aware that he was spending large parts of the day braced for danger, while also carrying the guilt of the memory and the sense that the world could not be relied upon. His most persistent belief was that people cannot be trusted and that the world is a dangerous place, a conclusion that sat heavily over even his most ordinary routines. What finally brought him to treatment was the recognition that he no longer wanted his life to keep shrinking around these fears. He hoped for enough relief to sit through a conversation without rehearsing every line, to smell something burnt without being pulled back into that moment, and to be able to look at a uniform without feeling that old betrayal rise up in him again. What he feared most was that nothing would change and that he would go on living as though danger were always one step away.
